title: When the Weather Turns, Taming the Perfect Storm Class
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele defines a 'perfect storm' class — a rare adverse combination of a high concentration of SEN and behavioural needs, significant prior-attainment gaps in the subject, and a tight friendship group whose mutual protection turns individual disruption into a collective phenomenon. His claim is that in such a class even trivial content fails to land, because students are not attending or retaining, and he uses the collapse of an explanation as simple as 3a + 2a = 5a to make the point. The governing principle, borrowed from Adam Boxer, is that poor behaviour is a lead weight on school improvement and there is little point in fixing anything else first; following Ollie Lovell and Mark Dowley's Classroom Management Handbook, he treats behaviour as a subject to be taught. The strategy is 'Stop, Teach, and Repeat': stop the lesson with pens down and immediate sanctions for non-compliance, escalate to a full physical reset with students standing silently behind chairs where needed, then calmly explain why you stopped, teach the behaviour policy point by point, and cold call a student to restate the expectation. He is candid that students will complain and that compliant students lose time, and argues that this is the point — the deliberate cost is what makes non-compliant students conclude that following the rules is the fastest route back to normal. He closes with his own case: line up, greet by name, silent entry, a silent stand-off, and four deliberate resets that bought three weeks without one.
points: The diagnostic is the piece's most portable element: three named ingredients — behavioural need, skill gaps, and a mutually protective friendship group — distinguish a perfect storm from a merely tricky class.
Behaviour is framed as curriculum, not as a precondition to be wished for, which is what licenses spending lesson time explicitly teaching the policy point by point.
The escalation ladder is graded — pens down and listen for in-lesson dips, standing silently behind chairs for a chaotic start — so the full reset retains its force.
Cold-calling a student to repeat the key expectation is the check for understanding applied to behaviour rather than content.
Emanuele treats the lost learning time as a deliberate investment with a measurable payoff, reporting four uses of the stand-up reset followed by three weeks without needing it.
quotes: As teachers, we’ve all had challenging classes. But every few years, we encounter one that goes beyond the usual “tricky” group: a perfect storm.

The core result of this “storm” is that learning is completely disrupted. When you’re constantly battling low-level (or high-level) chaos, even the simplest explanation, like 3a + 2a = 5a, can be met with confusion because students are not truly attending or retaining.

Inspired by the work of Ollie Lovell and Dr. Mark Dowley in The Classroom Management Handbook, we must treat behaviour as a subject to be taught, just like any other. You cannot teach content until you have excellent behavior, because any disruption prevents all students from grasping the material, making your effective teaching strategies (like Explicit Instruction or Mini Whiteboards) useless.
You need to be brave and proactive. When behavior dips to a level where excellent learning is clearly impossible, you must stop.
You must be prepared to repeat this process as often as necessary. Yes, students will get bored and complain, particularly those who are behaving. But this is the entire point.

I recently faced this with my own “perfect storm” class. Chaotic entry routines meant students weren’t settled for 8+ minutes. My original attempts to fix it before students enter failed as my room is located in a busy, loud corridor.
It’s tedious at first, but it saves time in the long run. After four deliberate, repeated uses of the Stand Up reset at the start of a lesson, I haven’t had to use it for the last three weeks.
